recipes.source_use_case_name: Service contract stewardship across a project's merge waves
recipes.name: Service contract stewardship across a project's merge waves
recipes.description: A project agrees what every one of its services must carry, and then ships anyway. The list lives in a design document, the services are built by different hands weeks apart, and nothing compares the two until an audit or an incident does it. Each missing piece is individually small, which is exactly why none of them is ever the reason to stop: a service without a rollback note, one whose published contract no longer matches the routes it serves, one whose events go out with no consumer anywhere. The obligations are only visible together, and only just before something merges, because after the merge the project has already agreed to carry them. Before a wave of work merges, read every service in the project against the contract the project declared, obligation by obligation, and decide for each service whether it is certified, certified with named gaps, or not certified at all. File each missing obligation as an idea naming the obligation it violates and the service it belongs to, rather than fixing it inside the certification. Refuse to certify against a contract that does not exist: an undeclared contract is the finding, and the wave stops on it.

recipes.source_use_case_name: Threat model and evidence custody for a money path project
recipes.name: Threat model and evidence custody for a money path project
recipes.description: This work is for money path projects only, and it says so because the cost of holding it everywhere is that it is held nowhere. A threat model is written once, at the moment somebody asks for one, and then the service it describes keeps moving: a new caller, a token that now crosses a boundary it did not cross before, a queue that a second consumer joined. The document does not move with it, so within two quarters the model describes a system that no longer exists while still reading as current. The same happens to the evidence a project claims: a control is named, the artefact behind it was never produced, and nobody notices because a claim and an artefact look identical in a list. Keep a current threat model for every money path service in this project, and treat a change that moves a trust boundary as a change to the model in the same act rather than as a follow up. Then check the models against reality in the other direction: every claim a model makes about a control has to resolve to something that exists, and every piece of evidence this project has promised has to be an artefact somebody can open, or be written down as a named gap.

recipes.source_use_case_name: Codebase stewardship by a maintenance worker the owner scopes
recipes.name: Codebase stewardship by a maintenance worker the owner scopes
recipes.description: A project that only ever adds behaviour accrues the debt nobody was asked to pay: modules that grew past the shape they were designed for, three copies of one helper, a build that takes a minute longer each month, dependencies pinned to versions with known holes, and test suites that pass while covering less than they did. None of it is an accepted idea, because nobody files 'the code is worse than it needs to be' as a finding, and the owner's delivery capacity is spent on the ideas that were filed. The work is real, mechanical, and well suited to a cheaper engine than the one that decides what the project is for. Carry ONE bounded maintenance scope the owner wrote: a refactor that keeps behaviour, a structural rebalance of files and modules, a technical-design upgrade the owner named, a dependency or toolchain move, or a coverage or build-time repair. Read the code and the gates before touching anything, make the change on its own branch in small commits, keep every test and gate green without editing a gate or deleting a test, and stop at the scope's edge with a note for the owner about what lies past it.
